posts.content_md:
I've been having a problem with these, and would like to ask the following question:

Are small (~1 to 3mm) parallel lines in the plane of the emulsion always caused by interference effects from reflections from the glass and/or gelatin?

These lines are clean and straight. They are on the plane of the emulsion, not the object. I've been having them especially since using green light, and my green laser does have a number of optics after it: a beam attenuator (metallized beamsplitter), three beam-shaping lenses, and a half-wave plate. The lines are never visible on the spread beam, only in the hologram, so I doubt the optics are causing the problem, but I'm not at all sure.

> **Joe Farina:** I do have one of Sam's dongles with two green LED's, the second one comes on reliably every time. If a second mode is present, I assumed the object would be banded (maybe mode-hopping and multiple modes show different effects?), but these lines are always in the plane of the emulsion. Thanks for the comments, I think this is probably a polarization issue, but I could also try adjusting the power of the 315.

Hi, Joe.

If it is 'woods grain' effect, I think it should show variations in direction as emulsion thickness change. Or your emulsion is perfect, or something else is in question.

If it is recorded at the Brewster's angle, then there should be no such grain. Note that such angle is slightly different for red and green laser. Do you record your hologram at Brewster angle at all?

To inspect whether bad polarization is an issue, use blank glass plate, and put in your plate holder. If there is any reflected light, then it is not set at Brewster's angle, or polarization is not correct (P-polarization). For two wavelengths (red and green), you may chose slight change in angle so that both lasers has the least reflection from both surfaces. 

If multimode or mode hopping is present in green laser, then there should be difference on the object; red one without banding, green one banded. I am not sure in difference between multimode and mode hopping, because my blue laser has both, so I really don't know what to blame for that if I get banded hologram. But, as you said, I saw banding only on the object, not on the emulsion. 

Best--

milan

I know that laser light, when not correctly polarized (and at Brewster's angle), can bounce around inside the glass (and gelatin), and I assume this is the reason for those lines. posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md: Just to update, all those lines were simply due to bad housekeeping on my part. Once the polarizations were correctly aligned, and the glass was at 57 degrees to the beam, no more lines. 50 degrees is ok too. At 45 degrees, some fine lines begin to appear.
